name: Bondage versus freedom / passions versus adequate ideas
plain_explanation: We are 'in bondage' when what happens to us is caused by things outside us and we do not understand why; we become 'free' as we understand our own emotions clearly, because a clearly and distinctly understood emotion stops being a passive 'passion.'
precise_definition: Freedom, for Spinoza, consists in being self-determined through adequate understanding rather than driven by external causes grasped only through confused, inadequate ideas; an emotion ceases to be a 'passion' once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
why_it_mattered: This is the psychological engine of Spinoza's ethics: intellectual understanding, not willpower or unselfishness, is presented as the remedy for destructive emotion.
historical_origin: Developed in the fourth and fifth books of the Ethics, 'Of Human Bondage' and 'Of the Power of the Understanding.'
examples: Hatred, once clearly understood in relation to its causes, loses its grip on the mind.
Hope and fear are condemned as irrational because they treat the future, which is really as fixed as the past, as uncertain.
competing_positions: The Stoics' rejection of all emotion, which Russell notes Spinoza does not share - Spinoza objects only to 'passions,' not to all feeling.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Compared by Russell to Socrates and Plato's view that wrong action stems from intellectual error.
